newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Central Bank liberalises financial sector.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Central Bank liberalises financial sector.

text.p: Jordan's Central Bank Governor Ziyad Fariz announced on Wednesday a major easing of controls on foreign currency deposits that should allow banks to invest more than $700 million in international capital markets.

He said the bank was slashing reserve requirements -- the percentage of bank deposits which must be placed with the Central Bank -- on foreign currency deposits and removing a ceiling on foreign currency accounts held by Jordanians.

"This is a very important step towards full liberalisation of money and capital markets that will enhance the effectiveness and profitabilty of banks and encourage local and foreign investment in the Jordanian economy," Fariz told Reuters.
Bankers say the new rules will allow banks to increase their profitability by investing in higher yield debt instruments and utilising more of their foreign currency holdings.
The bank reduced a compulsory reserve requirement on foreign currency deposits with local banks to 14 percent from 35 percent, according to a bank circular obtained by Reuters.
The move in effect will release around $700 million that the Central Bank was holding. Banks can now invest it in both the domestic market and international capital markets.

Foreign currency accounts in Jordanian banks hold 2.367 billion dinars ($3.34 billion). Bank deposits, both local and foreign currency accounts, totalled 5.973 billion dinars ($8.44 billion) in August.

In a move aimed at nudging Jordan's quiet interbank money market, the Central Bank further eased the reserve requirements by allowing banks to place one-fifth of the new reserve levels on local interbank markets, provided they could still cover the full reserve requirements at the end of each month.

The bank also removed a ceiling equivalent to 500,000 dinars ($706,000) on foreign currency deposits which a Jordanian can hold in domestic banks. It will allow the banks to invest those foreign currency deposits in international capital markets and enter into foreign currency margin trading.
These options were previously restricted to foreign currency accounts held by non-resident Jordanians.
Asset swap operations for Jordanian resident accounts would no longer need the approval of the Central Bank.
"It will allow banks to develop their resources more efficiently," said Fariz.
A partial liberalisation last year allowed banks to invest only non-resident accounts foreign currency holdings in some international corporate bond issues government bonds.
